newsitem.title: USA: China's Qian in Washington, set to meet Albright. [CORRECTED 19:41 GMT]
newsitem.headline: China's Qian in Washington, set to meet Albright. [CORRECTED 19:41 GMT]

text.p: (Corrects name in headline to Qian from Qichen.)
Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen arrived on Monday for talks on Hong Kong, arms sales and other topics in preparation for a U.S.-China summit later this year.

Qian was opening two-days of top-level Washington talks on Monday afternoon by meeting Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, just a week after the United States hosted two prominent critics of Beijing: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Martin Lee and the Dalai Lama, spiritual leader of Tibet.
That backdrop alone underscored the sensitive issues Washington must balance as it pursues better ties with China.
Qian's mission followed a highly successful Russia-China summit, and comes amid continuing controversy over alleged attempts by Beijing to buy influence in U.S. elections.
Qian was to spend most of Monday in meetings and a working dinner with Albright, and would meet President Bill Clinton before leaving Washington on Wednesday.

The visit is aimed at making progress toward a summit later this year between Clinton and Chinese President Jiang Zemin and at promoting a bilateral effort to improve still prickly relations through increased exchange visits and cooperation.

U.S. officials predicted no dramatic breakthroughs in the Qian talks but stressed the need to make progress on major areas of concern, like weapons proliferation, so as to ensure the summit has concrete achievements, not just rhetoric.

Hong Kong will figure in prominently, owing to the fast approaching reversion of the British colony to China's control on July 1. In line with an intensifying U.S. effort, Albright will press Qian to maintain the colony's civil and political liberties, which critics say are already eroding.

U.S. officials will also urge China to encourage North Korea to enter into four-party peace talks. The effort stalled last week when North Korea tied its participation to more food aid, lifting U.S. sanctions and diplomatic recognition.
Among the summit goals is to get to a point where Clinton could authorise implementation of a 1985 peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement that would give Beijing access to advanced U.S. technology.

But to do that, China would have to greatly improve export controls, among other steps. U.S. officials say Beijing has done little toward this goal, part of a 1996 commitment, but it is still conceiveable China could take sufficient action by the summit to warrant implementing the PNC accord.
Qian last met Albright on her Feb. 24 trip to China. Since then, Vice President Al Gore also visited Beijing, drawing criticism at home for not being tough enough on human rights.

In addition, recent reports that top Chinese officials may have approved attempts to influence U.S. elections through 1996 campaign donations has caused a furore and clouded the debate over renewing China's most-favoured-nation trade status.

Clinton urged no judgment against Beijing on the political interference allegations until all the facts are in. But he restated the administration's position that if such activity were proven it could have serious consequences for U.S.-China ties, which have begun to improve after six difficult years.
Even so, U.S. officials seem confident they can persuade Congress to renew MFN trade benefits for China for one year.
